name: Fuel cost
seoTitle: Fuel cost Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Fuel cost: work out fuel efficiency/consumption (mileage) from the one-way distance and the fuel price at your gas station. A free everyday life…
summary: Give the Fuel cost calculator the one-way distance, the fuel price at your gas station and the fuel used during this trip and it returns fuel efficiency/consumption (mileage). It is built for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Fuel cost calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fuel cost calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports fuel efficiency/consumption (mileage) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the one-way distance, the fuel price at your gas station and the fuel used during this trip.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in kilometers. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Two-way trip”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in US Dollar. The unit chip switches it to any of the 113 supported units.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “I don't know my car's fuel efficiency”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in liters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 40 supported units.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fuel cost calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Fuel efficiency/consumption (mileage)=one-way distance × two way ÷ fuel used during this trip
Fuel cost=fuel used during this trip × fuel price at your gas station
Fuel efficiency/consumption (mileage)=distance driven ÷ fuel put into the tank
Distance driven=one-way distance × fuel put into the tank × two way ÷ fuel used during this trip

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in liters per 100 kilometers, and convertible to any of the 10 units on that chip.
  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.
  • Shown in liters, and convertible to any of the 40 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilometers, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Fuel economy, opening in liters per 100 kilometers
  • Volume, opening in liters
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Volume, opening in liters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fuel cost calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the one-way distance, the fuel price at your gas station and the fuel used during this trip — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Fuel cost calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns fuel efficiency/consumption (mileage), derived from the one-way distance, the fuel price at your gas station and the fuel used during this trip. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fuel cost calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the one-way distance, the fuel price at your gas station and the fuel used during this trip, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter one-way distance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. One-way distance opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Fuel cost calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
